newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea central bank acts to halt won's slump.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea central bank acts to halt won's slump.

text.p: South Korea's central bank on Tuesday sent a stern signal to currency speculators as the local currency fell to an all-time low, dealers and economists said.
"The Bank of Korea sent out a strong warning to speculators to prevent further depreciation of the won," said Lee In-hyung, a senior economist of LG Economic Research Institute.

In what has become a pattern recently, the central bank intervened in the interbank market in morning trading shortly after the won fell to a record low of 901.00 per dollar at 0130 GMT, traders said. It stepped in again in the afternoon.
The bank, as usual, refused to confirm the action, but the won ended at 897.60 on Tuesday against 898.70 on Monday.
"The central bank is set on alleviating fears of a currency crisis at an early stage," said Lee.
Aiding the won's rebound, an assistant governor of the central bank said he believed the dollar had peaked against the won under the current demand and supply situation.
"Considering the prospects for short- and long-term demand and the supply of dollars, the dollar seems to have peaked versus the won," assistant governor Lee Kang-nam said.
The volatility in the foreign exchange market also sent jitters through Seoul's other financial markets, pushing bond yields higher and stock prices lower.

Yields on both three-year benchmark corporate bonds rose to 12.32 percent on Tuesday from 12.25 percent on Monday, despite the central bank's release of 500 billion won ($557 million) through two-day repurchase agreements on Monday.
Dealers said market liquidity would remain tight until the Korean Thanksgiving holiday next month, when corporate demand for cash is traditionally high.
Stock prices slipped with the composite index closing 6.00 points lower at 741.29 as the weakening won and rising interest rates dampened sentiment.
"The won's steep fall against the dollar raised concerns about the nation's whole financial market," said Lee Young-won, a broker at Daewoo Securities.
Analysts and dealers blame a recent string of corporate troubles which led to difficulties in overseas borrowing of foreign currencies and rising exchange rate vulnerability.
"Fears that the Korean won could fall under speculators' attack have prompted domestic firms to sell won and buy dollars," said Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investment Securities.
Lee of LG Economic Research Institute said: "Financial institutions and corporations are competitively securing dollars on expectations of further financial troubles at local companies and banks."
A corporate crisis which started with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January has led to downward revisions of the international credit ratings of local debt-laden financial institutions.
Traders said the volatility of Southeast Asian currencies has also led to speculative selling of the won.
Economists said while the volatility was hurting sentiment towards the won it was not having a direct impact.
"Most importantly, the won is not considered to be overvalued like other Southeast Asian currencies. On the contrary, it has depreciated considerably since last year," said LG's Lee.
The won fell 8.2 percent against the dollar last year and a further 5.9 percent so far this year.
But restrictions on speculative short-selling by foreigners, the won's 2.25 percent trading band and its lack of convertibility would limit excessive speculation, economists said.
